 The 6 New Rules For Flying Without A REAL ID

 Felix Ngeso is a travel writer covering topics related to transportation, national parks, and scenic outdoor travel. His passion for travel began in university, when time outside the classroom gave him the freedom to discover how different places, landscapes, and experiences could be from what he was used to. Since then, he has explored unique places across the U.S., shaping his approach to destination storytelling.
In addition to contributing to TheTravel, Felix is a co-founder of a tour company that helps travelers choose destinations based on their interests and design the perfect itineraries. When he is not writing, he can be found camping, taking solo scenic road trips, or discovering new travel gems.

 Since May 7, 2025, Americans aged 18 and older have needed a REAL ID-compliant license , a state ID , or another TSA-accepted document to clear security for domestic flights. However, your REAL ID might not get you through TSA in 2026 , and the federal requirement does not mean every passenger must obtain it.

 A valid U.S. passport , passport card , Global Entry card , military ID , or permanent resident card can also satisfy the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) requirements. Travelers without a compliant state ID can continue flying without applying for one, provided they have an accepted alternative.
 Passengers who arrive without any acceptable identification have another option. Introduced on February 1, 2026, TSA ConfirmID has let passengers pay $45 for an alternative identity check that covers a 10-day travel window . From accepted alternatives and digital identification to additional screening procedures and exemptions for children, here are six essential rules to understand before flying without a REAL ID.

 Posts 
 1 
 By  
 Lauren Feather 
 Travelers Can Use The U.S. Passport Instead Of A REAL ID
 Passenger holding a U.S. passport on a plane Credit: KieferPix / Shutterstock.com (Gemini-Enhanced) 
 A U.S. passport, which can be renewed online under specific rules , is the simplest substitute for a REAL ID at a TSA checkpoint. The passport book and the wallet-size passport card are accepted for domestic flights, even when the traveler’s driver’s license is not REAL ID-compliant. TSA also honors either document for up to one year after its expiration date, which helps travelers who have not yet renewed.
 Other alternatives TSA also accepts include DHS Trusted Traveler cards ( Global Entry, NEXUS, SENTRI, and FAST ), Department of Defense IDs , including those issued to dependents, and Permanent Resident Cards . Foreign government-issued passports, photo IDs issued by federally recognized Tribal Nations , and Transportation Worker Identification Credentials (TWIC) also qualify. Residents of Michigan, Minnesota, New York, Vermont, and Washington can use a state-issued Enhanced Driver’s License too.
 However, some documents will not work, including a temporary paper license issued while a new card is in the mail. A standard license that fails REAL ID standards is also not accepted on its own. Before heading to the airport, travelers should confirm their document appears on TSA’s acceptable ID list.
 Some Travelers Can Use Approved Digital Identification At Airport Security
 Smartphone screen showing a digital ID card in Apple Wallet Credit:  Evgenia Parajanian /Shutterstock 
 A mobile driver’s license (mDL) can replace a physical card at TSA checkpoints , which is one of the eight rules that changed for U.S. travelers in 2026 . However, it must only come from a participating state and is based on a REAL ID, Enhanced Driver’s License, or Enhanced ID. That rules out a state mDL for anyone holding a standard, non-compliant license. The checkpoint must also have a CAT-2 credential reader, though TSA says digital IDs are accepted at more than 250 airports.
 A passport-based digital ID is the better option for travelers without a REAL ID. TSA accepts Apple Digital ID , Google ID Pass , CLEAR ID , and Samsung ID with CLEAR , each built from a U.S. passport and meant for domestic travel. TSA lists these under its ongoing testing efforts, meaning acceptance can vary by checkpoint.
 A photo of a license saved on a phone does not count, and the Digital ID does not replace the physical document. According to the TSA , travelers must still carry their physical ID and keep the passport or another accepted card on hand in case a reader fails.
 Passengers Without Acceptable Identification Can Pay $45 For TSA ConfirmID
 TSA officer handling REAL ID to a traveler Credit: Shutterstock 
 Travelers aged 18 and older who reach a checkpoint without a REAL ID or any other accepted document can pay $45 to use TSA ConfirmID, which began on February 1, 2026 . The fee only applies to people with no acceptable ID . TSA then attempts to confirm the traveler’s identity, but the fee is nonrefundable even if that attempt fails.
 The payment covers 10 days starting from the travel start date entered at checkout, so setting it to the first flight covers a return trip too. Passengers can use the same payment confirmation for multiple flights within that period, provided they meet the program’s requirements. Each adult without ID must pay and register separately, though someone else can make the payment as long as the traveler’s legal name is entered correctly.
 All payments go through the U.S. Treasury’s payment portal using a credit card, debit card, bank account (ACH), PayPal, or Venmo. Cash is not accepted at the airport. After payment, Pay.gov emails a receipt, which must be shown on a phone or in print at the checkpoint. TSA recommends paying before leaving for the airport because a traveler who cannot produce the receipt may have to pay again.
 Paying The ConfirmID Fee Does Not Guarantee Permission To Fly
 A Transaction successful notification on smart phone Credit:  KGBR /Shutterstock 
 Paying $45 buys an attempt at identity verification, not a pass through security. Still, TSA officers must confirm who the traveler is at the checkpoint, and travelers will need to provide additional information. Passengers whose identity cannot be confirmed, who decline to cooperate, or who withhold identification will be denied entry to the screening area. Additionally, the fee is not returned.
 The process can also take longer than presenting an accepted identification document. According to DHS, the process typically takes 10 to 15 minutes but can run 30 minutes or more. Travelers without a receipt must first pay through the payment portal, which can be done on a phone at the airport, though TSA urges paying ahead. Passengers may also face additional screening, which matters when boarding is close.
 Although ConfirmID is optional, travelers without an acceptable ID who skip it cannot proceed. The safest approach is to arrive extra early, which is one of the top tips shared by a former TSA officer on navigating airport security , and keep the Pay.gov receipt ready on a phone or on paper. Travelers should also check that the legal name and start date are correct before paying, because TSA uses the receipt to begin verification. Whenever possible, travelers can carry an accepted physical ID, so verification never becomes necessary.
 Children Under 18 Do Not Need REAL ID To Fly Domestically
 Little girl at the airport Credit:  Irina WS /Shutterstock 
 TSA does not require travelers under 18 to show any identification on domestic flights , so a child needs no REAL ID, passport, or other card to clear security. Parents do not need to get one just for a domestic trip. When a child travels with an adult, the adult’s ID is what the TSA checks . That adult still needs an acceptable document. A parent without one gets no exemption from the child’s rule and must show another accepted ID or pay for Confirm.ID, even if the children with them need nothing.
 However, two exceptions apply. A child flying alone who has TSA PreCheck needs an acceptable ID to get PreCheck screening. Airlines also set their own rules for minors. Unaccompanied minor programs often require a completed form, contact details for the person picking the child up, and sometimes proof of age such as a birth certificate . Families using PreCheck should also know that children 12 and under can join a parent in the lane, while teens 13 to 17 need the PreCheck indicator on their own boarding pass.
 Families should check both TSA screening rules and their airline’s policies before departure to avoid unexpected problems at the airport.
 Travelers Should Upgrade Their State IDs Before Their Next Domestic Flight
 driving licenses from different USA states Credit:  Mehaniq /Shutterstock 
 Travelers who regularly fly within the United States can skip ConfirmID entirely by switching to a REAL ID-compliant driver’s license or state ID card. Each state’s DMV sets its own fees, appointment rules, and accepted documents. For travelers planning to apply, the state agency’s website is the best place to start. Some states let applicants pre-submit documents online, but the first REAL ID must be completed in person because staff verifies original paperwork .
 Applicants bring the following:
 Proof of identity : a birth certificate or U.S. passport
 Proof of a Social Security number : a Social Security card or W-2
 Two proofs of current home address : such as a utility bill, bank statement, or lease
 Legal name change papers : certified documents, if your current name differs from your records
 Compliant cards carry a star in the upper portion of the card , though the color and design vary by state, and Enhanced Driver’s Licenses use a flag marking instead .
 Before booking, travelers should check their license for the star and look at its expiration date, since renewal is a natural time to switch. A valid passport or passport card still works if a traveler already owns one, but a REAL ID means they do not have to carry it for domestic trips.
